messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Approaching a multivariate ODE fit with missing data
parts:
ODEs aren't any different than other parts of Stan for
missing data.

The first thing to do is think about what the model would look
like if you had all the data. Then you take the missing data and
declare it as parameters. It's a strategy that's outlined in
the missing data chapter of the manual and will work for any
Bayesian application.

If you give us some more specifics of your problem, we might be
able to provide more concrete advice---I didn't know what to make
of two lines of data with some missing elements---where does it
fit into your ODE model?

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Approaching a multivariate ODE fit with missing data
parts:
There’s nothing special about the missing data here.  You just
solve the ODE for all measurement times, and then include a
measurement model only for those components that you do
measure at time point.  So sometimes you’d have a likelihood
contributes for each components, sometimes just a few.

If you want to impute those values then in generated quantities
you sample from the corresponding random number generator
(i.e. if your measurement model is Gaussian then use the
normal_rng) around the latent state.

Let’s go to a simpler example.  Let’s say that we have a two-dimensional
Gaussian with known covariance and we measure only the first component.
The corresponding Stan model would look something like

data {
  int N;
  vector[2] y[N];
  matrix[2, 2] Sigma;
}

parameters {
  real mu;
}

model {
  mu ~ normal(0, 1);
  for (n in 1:N)
    y[1] ~ normal(mu, Sigma[1, 1]);
}

In other words, we marginalize out over the unobserved components which
in the Gaussian case reduces to dropping any terms that depend on the
second component.

The important statistical concept here is that you can’t learn from unobserved 
data, all you can do it predict it.  So you want to build a model without the
unobserved components and if you really care about trying to figure out what
went on then you predict those components in the generated quantities block.

> On Nov 18, 2016, at 11:00 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> In other words, we marginalize out over the unobserved components which
> in the Gaussian case reduces to dropping any terms that depend on the

>
> The important statistical concept here is that you can’t learn from unobserved
> data, all you can do it predict it. So you want to build a model without the
> unobserved components and if you really care about trying to figure out what
> went on then you predict those components in the generated quantities block.

You can't learn from completely unobserved data, but you can
learn a bit from partially observed data (e.g., one or more of many
predictors is missing, or the outcome is missing). But like
Michael says, the trick is to provide a joint model for everything
as if it were all observed, then marginalize out what's missing. Sometimes
the easiest way to do that is to declare the missing quantity as a parameter.
Then you get a posterior that includes it, but if you ignore it, it amounts
to marginalizing it out. Sometimes the model is neatly formed and you
can marginalize analytically (this is common in multivariate normal models).

- Bob
